water-and-carbon-cycles: Plants pull vast amounts of carbon from the air every year. Why did the air's carbon stay level for millennia?
Only a tiny fraction of Earth's water is in the air at any moment. So how does it keep raining?
At any moment, rivers hold only about 0.006% of Earth's fresh water. So how does a river keep flowing through weeks without rain?

On 23 December 2013, 43–45 mm of rain fell on two river basins in southern England. Within a day, one river surged to one of its highest flows since records began; the other barely rose, and peaked only in mid-February after weeks more rain. Why did the same storm have such different effects?
A study found that urbanisation made Hurricane Harvey-scale flooding in Houston's basins about 21 times as likely in 2017. How can a city make a flood worse?
Most of Earth's carbon is locked away in rock. How does any of it get back into the air?
Volcanoes and wildfires have always released carbon. What has changed the carbon cycle so fast?
Since 1979 the Arctic has warmed nearly four times as fast as the planet as a whole. Why there?

In May 2024 a company opened what it called the world's largest plant for pulling CO₂ out of the air, in Iceland, designed to capture up to 36,000 tonnes a year. Could machines like it clean up our emissions?
Clear the Amazon's trees and the streams run fuller. So why could the region end up drier?
Two Welsh hillsides get almost the same rain. Why does the forested one send less water downstream?
hot-desert-systems-and-landscapes: Some desert dunes hold sand that has travelled thousands of kilometres. Where does desert sand come from?
Antarctica is covered in ice, yet it counts as a desert. How?
The Atacama lies right beside the Pacific Ocean, yet it is the driest desert on Earth. How?
Sand covers only about 20% of the world's deserts. What shapes the rest?
Egypt's Great Sphinx may have been carved from a rock ridge that nature had already shaped. What shaped it?
Deserts are defined by a lack of water. So why are so many desert landforms made by water?
Between 11,000 and 5,000 years ago, the Sahara had permanent lakes, plants and people. Today it is desert. Did people cause the change?
In the Namib, a river that flows only every few years stops a sea of giant dunes. How can that be?
Farmers turned bare, crusted ground back into fields and forest. Will it hold in a hotter future?
coastal-systems-and-landscapes: The Holderness cliffs have been crumbling into the North Sea for centuries. Where does all that material go?
Between 1951 and 2004 the cliffs at Aldbrough, on England's Holderness coast, retreated about 2 m a year. Why do they disappear so fast?
In 1990 an Australian sea arch fell, stranding two visitors on a new island. How does the sea make islands?
Spurn Point is over three miles long and in places only 50 m wide. How did a finger of sand form across the mouth of the Humber?
Bare, sticky mud is flooded by tide after tide. How does it turn into a meadow that cattle can graze?
On the coast of the Gulf of Bothnia, the land rises out of the sea by about 0.9 m a century. Elsewhere, coasts are drowning. How can both be true?
By 2014 the Environment Agency had built new banks inland at Medmerry, West Sussex, and let the sea flood the land between. Why give land to the sea?
A clay cliff can barely move one year, then lose metres the next. How do you find its real rate of retreat?
The sea is wrecking the rock towers that millions of visitors come to see. Should anyone try to stop it?
glacial-systems-and-landscapes: Glaciers exist on every continent except Australia. What decides where cold environments are found?
Some glaciers race forward metres a day. Others, frozen to their beds, barely move. Why the difference?
Between 1941 and 2004, Alaska's Muir Glacier retreated 12 km. All that time, its ice kept flowing towards the sea. How can both be true?
How can a ridge of river gravel wind uphill and over hills, when rivers only flow downhill?
Near Tuktoyaktuk in Arctic Canada, a 49 m hill rises out of flat tundra. Its core is solid ice. How did it form?
Yosemite's Lembert Dome has a gentle slope on one side and a steep face on the other. Why?
A 16,500-tonne boulder sits on the flat prairie of Alberta, Canada, far from the mountains it came from. How did it get there?
Dust and floodwater beside Arctic oil roads can thaw frozen ground. Why are cold places so easily harmed?
Shishmaref, an Iñupiaq village on an Alaskan island, has voted three times to move. Why, and why is it still there?
Darwin spent hours in a Welsh mountain hollow and missed what was all around him. What did he miss?
In May 2025 a glacier buried much of the Swiss village of Blatten. Why did only one person die?
hazards: In earthquake-prone California, most homeowners' policies do not cover earthquakes. Why not?
Why do some disasters leave a community better prepared, and others leave it worse off for years?
The Atlantic is about 2.5 cm wider every year. What moves the plates?
Iceland is splitting, the Andes are rising and California slides sideways. What happens where plates meet?
In 1985 a volcano 45 km away killed about 23,000 people in Armero, two hours after it erupted. How?
About 1,600 magnitude-5 earthquakes strike each year, and about one magnitude-8. Which should planners prepare for?
On Fuego, in 2018, a golf resort evacuated safely. A village two kilometres further on was buried. Why?
After a 2004 earthquake off Sumatra, people died in 10 countries around the Indian Ocean. How?
Nepal 2015 and Kaikōura 2016 were both magnitude 7.8. One killed more than 8,790 people; the other killed 2. Why?
Large earthquakes are not becoming more common. So why do experts expect more people to be affected by geophysical disasters?
By 2013, Hong Kong said it had cut the landslide risk from its man-made slopes by about 75%. Is preventing disasters worth more than responding to them?
ecosystems-under-stress: Monitored wildlife populations have shrunk by almost three-quarters since 1970. Why should people care?
Cut down a rainforest and its soil soon fails. If the forest was so rich, where were its riches kept?
Since the 1950s, many upper-ocean species have moved towards the poles by about 52 km every decade. Why move, and what happens to living things and farms on land?
Tundra and hot desert both get very little rain, yet they look nothing alike. What sorts the world's biomes?
Darwin and Manaus are both hot all year. Why is one surrounded by savanna and the other by rainforest?
Clearing tropical forest and savanna brings farms, jobs and food. Who gains, and what is lost?
For half the year it pours; for the other half almost nothing falls. How does life cope in the savanna?
global-systems-and-global-governance: The Netherlands tops the KOF Globalisation Index. The USA, the world's largest economy at market exchange rates, ranks 28th. How can that be?
In 2023 the Panama Canal cut the number of ships it let through. In 2026 conflict choked oil shipping through the Strait of Hormuz. Has technology really made the world "shrink"?
In 2024 one inflow of money into Tajikistan equalled almost half of its GDP. Which flows matter most, and for which places?
In 2025 China's economy was larger than the USA's by one IMF measure and smaller by another. Which country is the superpower?
Two farmers grow the same crop. One sells it tax-free in Europe; the other pays a tariff. Why?

Apple employs about 166,000 people. Toyota and its affiliates run more than 50 manufacturing operations in 27 countries and regions outside Japan. Why do these two giants make their products in such different ways?
China imported about ten times as many soybeans in 2023 as in 2000. In 2025, nearly three in four came from Brazil. Why does what people eat in China matter to land in Brazil?
There is no world government. So who makes the rules that hold the global economy together?
In 2022 Sri Lanka defaulted on its foreign debt and turned to the IMF. Who sets the terms of rescue loans, and is there an alternative?
Krill from the Southern Ocean ends up in supplements and fish feed. Who loses if it is overfished?
No police patrol Antarctica. So how are its rules on fishing, whaling and mining enforced?

Between 1970 and 2008 the share of world trade in world GDP more than doubled. Since then it has stalled, moving between about 52% and 62% to 2024, and nationalist politics has grown. Is globalisation creating its own backlash?
changing-places: Is a place just a dot on a map, or something more?
When a steelworks owned from Thailand shut, why did a town in England feel it?
18.5 million people born in India live in other countries, more than from any other country. How do they change places at both ends?
A poet begged bombs to fall on a town. Can a poem change how a real place is seen and treated?
Why would a city spend millions on a year of art?
Your street has a story no map tells. How do you uncover what made your own place what it is?
A crowded ward on the edge of a global city: how do you study a place thousands of miles away?
contemporary-urban-environments: In 1979 Shenzhen was what its government calls "a small backward border town". By 2024 it had 17.98 million residents. Where did they all come from?
In Denmark, 200 people can make a place urban. In Japan it takes 50,000. So how urban is the world?
Detroit had 1,849,568 people in 1950 and 639,111 in 2020. What emptied the Motor City?
Docklands, the Olympics, levelling up: forty years of urban policy. Has any of it closed the gap?
A square metre of land in Ginza, central Tokyo, is valued at ¥67.1 million. A square metre of housing land in Ome, also in Tokyo, averages ¥98,600. Why the gap?
A London estate of 1,212 homes was knocked down to make way for 3,000 new ones. Who is the new city for?
In 2011, 1 in 10 people in Mumbai's D ward lived in slums. In M/East ward, more than 3 in 4 did. Why such a gap inside one city?
Two neighbourhoods on two continents: both were demolished and redeveloped. Who decides what replaces a neighbourhood?
population-and-the-environment: Why do more than 9 in 10 people in China live on one side of a single line?
In 2023 the world's food supply came to about 3,000 calories per person per day. So why did around 645 million people go hungry in 2025?
An average UK wheat field yields about twice the world average. What makes one field out-produce another?
Deserts cover vast areas, yet few people live in them. Does climate decide where people live and farm?
Some of the world's best farm soils lie under grassland, not rainforest. Why?
Brazil left the UN's Hunger Map in 2014, fell back onto it, then left again in 2025. What does it take to end hunger, and to keep it ended?
In 2000, non-communicable diseases caused 58% of the world's deaths. In 2023 they caused 74%. Good news or bad news?
Two villages share a hillside in Kenya's highlands. Why might one have far more malaria than the other?
Malaria killed an estimated 610,000 people in 2024. Why does it kill mostly in one continent, and mostly young children?
In 1961 heart and circulatory disease caused over half of all UK deaths. Why has its death rate fallen so far?
resource-security: Is there a fixed amount of copper in the ground, or does it depend on who is counting?
In 2025, solar power generation grew by about 30%. In the same year, the world used more fossil fuel than ever. How can both be true?
Producing 1 kg of beef takes about 15,400 litres of water, on a world average. Is beef draining the world's rivers?

In March, April and May 2026, oil flows through the Strait of Hormuz averaged about 2.7 million barrels a day, down from about 20 million. Why did farmers and food importers far from the Gulf feel the shock?
In January 2018 Cape Town, a city of just over 4 million people, warned that its taps could be turned off in April: "Day Zero". What pushed it to the edge, and how did it pull back?
Hong Kong's own reservoirs supply only 20–30% of the water it uses. So how does it have water 24 hours a day?

The Lower Mekong's fisheries land an estimated 2.3 million tonnes of fish a year, worth about US$11 billion. Its hydropower capacity could more than double. Can one river be both a great fishery and a giant power station?
The Aral Sea was once the fourth-largest lake in the world. In 2014 the eastern part of its southern basin disappeared completely. What drained it?
About 85% of the Nile's water starts in Ethiopia, yet a 1959 agreement shared it between Egypt and Sudan. Who decides how it is used now, and what would make a deal work?
contemporary-urban-environments-part-2: A city is made of concrete, glass and roads. Can it really make its own weather?
In 2021 a coroner's report named air pollution exposure as a cause of a 9-year-old London girl's death. Who breathes a city's dirtiest air?
When rain falls on a city, where does it go, and why does it reach the river so fast?
A London brook was freed from its concrete channel. Did setting it loose make the area safer and greener?
In 2016, China reported importing about 8.8 million tonnes of plastic waste. In 2018, it imported about 51,000 tonnes. What happened, and where did the waste go?
Singapore burns the rubbish it can't recycle and buries the ash offshore. Why not simply landfill it all?
Smog, sewage and abandoned land: why do the same three problems need different fixes in different cities?
Urban areas use 75% of the world's energy. Vauban, a whole eco-district in Germany, is home to about 5,300 people. Can eco-cities and smart cities make a real difference?
Dhaka grew from 3 million people in 1980 to over 18 million by 2017. Who gains and who loses when a city grows that fast?
London is Britain's richest region. Is it also the best place in Britain to live?
ecosystems-under-stress-part-2: Leave bare rock and a pond untouched in lowland Britain for centuries. Why do both become similar woodland?
Heather moors look like wild nature. Why do people have to burn them to keep them?
Coral reefs cover a tiny part of the ocean floor. What decides where they can grow?
The Great Barrier Reef is called well managed. So why is its outlook still one of deterioration?
Someone planted a shrub to hold a sand dune in place. Why is it now being dug out?
Ranchers, miners and river families share the Amazon. Why does forest change hit each so differently?
hazards-part-2: Hurricane Ian hit Florida with 130-knot winds in 2022. Why was water, not wind, its deadliest hazard?
Why can a storm cost a rich country billions, yet kill far more people in a poor one?
A spark lands in dry grass. Why does one fire go out while another burns through a city?
When a wildfire reaches a city, what is lost besides the houses, and how do people recover?
Japan gets about a tenth of the world's earthquakes. How do more than 120 million people live with that?
A town sits beside a crack in the Earth that keeps erupting. How has the hazard reshaped the town?
population-and-the-environment-part-2: At today's rate, Niger's population would double in about 21 years. Japan's is shrinking. Why?
Can a falling birth rate make a country richer?
Within a year of August 2017, nearly 725,000 people had fled from Myanmar into Bangladesh. Why do so many people flee at once, and what happens where they arrive?
How many people can one planet, or one country, really support?
In 1798, Thomas Malthus argued that population would outrun food. Since 1961, the world's population has grown about 2.6 times. Has food per person risen or fallen?
Why might a thinner ozone layer show up in eye clinics, and a warmer climate in malaria wards?
From 1980 China limited most couples to one child. By 2021 it allowed three. Why the U-turn, and can governments change how many children people have?
The coast should be good for health, yet men in one seaside town can expect to live years less than England's average. How can a place harm health?
resource-security-part-2: About half of the 800-mile Trans-Alaska Pipeline runs above the ground. Why not bury all of it?
Britain once made almost three-quarters of its electricity from coal. What replaced it, and at what cost?
Acid rain was the big energy worry of the 1980s. Why do we hear so little about it today?
Over half the world's iron ore comes from just two countries. Why there, and who buys it?
Iron ore crosses an ocean before it becomes steel. Where along that journey does the damage happen?
Will the world run short of energy, water or metals, or will something change first?
Since 1970 the world has lost about 22% of its wetlands. Can a plan for a whole river basin bring a wetland back?

Singapore imports more than 90% of its food and makes about 95% of its electricity from imported gas. Jordan has about 61 m³ of renewable water per person a year. Which is more resource-secure, and why?
